own_scenes.desc: A finales de los ochenta el hip hop trajo un renacimiento del movimiento funk de los setenta: conciencia histórica, Malcolm X como héroe, Do the Right Thing y Boyz N the Hood, Yo! MTV Raps, In Living Color y el New Jack Swing. El rap sampleaba el funk porque venía del mismo sitio, la juventud rebelde del submundo urbano: EPMD con el bajo de «More Bounce to the Ounce» y Eric B. & Rakim con «I Know You Got Soul» de Bobby Byrd abrieron el frenesí de James Brown. La edad de oro empezó en 1988 con By All Means Necessary de BDP (KRS-One, autodidacta que perdió a Scott La Rock y montó «Self Destruction») y It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back de Public Enemy: bucles de ruido puro que llevaron el funk a la era digital, ataques a la industria y a los cantantes «sin espina», la oratoria de Chuck D y el bufón consciente Flavor Flav, con su reloj. «Fight the Power» (Do the Right Thing, 1989) quería, según Greg Tate, reconvocar el Black Power con el hip hop como medio; para Clinton eran lo que Dylan fue para el rock.

refs.q: Rap music has become the focal point of the resurgence of The Funk—a continuation of The Funk in the digital age.
refs.para: Rap music has become the focal point of the resurgence of The Funk—a continuation of The Funk in the digital age. By replicating original funk tracks, albeit in dehydrated form, Hip Hoppers have found themselves reiterating the stylistic and philosophical aspects of The Funk while repeating the groovy hooks. This should come as no surprise, since rap and funk both come from the same demographic group: the rebellious youth of the outcast urban underworld.
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Funk in the Nineties: Return of the Funk

refs.q: Public Enemy was like a slap in the face to a business that had grown complacent.
refs.para: Until this point, no one had taken on the monolithic strength, status, and illusory image of the music business this boldly. The eighties was a time when pop artists were crossing barriers and performing in “Aid” concerts worldwide, giving the industry an image of cooperation and freedom. Yet the process by which acts made it to the status of star in their particular fields was just as controlled as it was before. Public Enemy was like a slap in the face to a business that had grown complacent. The group won “Album of the Year” honors from the Village Voice Music Poll—a music award that generally goes to rock/pop superstars—and was nominated for the very Grammy Award they claimed to despise. (Public Enemy attended the Grammys that year, but the rap award went to D.J. Jazzy Jeff and the Fresh Prince.)
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Funk in the Nineties: Return of the Funk

refs.q: Flavor Flav was and is a fool, but a fool on a mission.
refs.para: Even their delivery was a significant breakthrough, for the duo of Chuck D (Carlton Ridenhour) and Flavor Flav (William Drayton), both of Long Island, delivered a classic one-two punch of cultural expression from within the tradition. Chuck was the insistent orator, serious and low in the range, dropping rhymes delivered with the controlled intensity of a Malcolm X speech, while Flavor Flav delivered the comic counterpoint, acting spastic and random. He rarely rhymed, but would always accentuate and strengthen Chuck D’s point. “Yea Boyeee!” was Flav’s main line, yet there was an endless supply of limericks and gimmicks. What was crucial to the partnership, it should be noted, is that Flavor Flav was a clown—in the tradition of the best black comics—yet he was a clown with consciousness, empowered with knowledge of self, an entirely different persona from the “Stepin Fetchit” and “Sambo” stereotypes of subservient and uncouth black Americans. Flavor Flav was and is a fool, but a fool on a mission. On the cover of Nation of Millions, he wears a gigantic clock as a medallion—a preposterous getup—yet it is designed to illustrate, through a comic medium, that time is indeed running out.
refs.chapter: Cap. 21: Funk in the Nineties: Return of the Funk

refs.q: Promoting a fearless disrespect for America’s institutions, Public Enemy was the embodiment of resistance for many who believed.
refs.para: Promoting a fearless disrespect for America’s institutions, Public Enemy was the embodiment of resistance for many who believed. Greg Tate wrote in 1988 that Public Enemy “wants to reconvene the black power movement with Hip Hop as the medium,” and he was right. Robert Christgau concurred in a 1990 Village Voice editorial: “Not even in the heyday of the … Clash has any group come so close to the elusive and perhaps ridiculous sixties rock ideal of raising political consciousness with music.” In so many ways, Public Enemy was attempting to do what rock, and The Funk, had attempted to do a generation earlier. George Clinton revered the group as truth-tellers of their generation in 1989: “To me they’re like what Bob Dylan was to rock and roll when they were starting to talk about the condition of the world. That’s Public Enemy now.” While allegations of anti-Semitism dogged the group at their peak, their impact caused a global Hip Hop movement to rise.
